messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Marco's Spiral

Marco Hernández was thirty-two when his younger brother died. The call came at three in the morning—a car accident on the interstate, his brother Diego pinned in the wreckage for forty minutes before the fire department extracted him. By the time the ambulance reached the hospital, there was nothing left to save. Marco had been working the night shift at the state penitentiary, walking the cellblocks in his uniform, and he learned the news in the parking lot afterward, his supervisor's hand on his shoulder, the words dissolving into static. He had not been there. He had not been able to stop it.

For the first few weeks, Marco moved through the world like a ghost. His wife, Catalina, watched him sit at the kitchen table for hours, staring at nothing. He returned to work because staying home felt worse—the house was full of Diego's absence, photographs he couldn't bear to see. But the prison became its own kind of trap. One afternoon in the second month, while processing intake paperwork in the administrative office, a news alert scrolled across the computer screen: a local story about a fatal accident, a young man killed instantly. Marco's vision narrowed. The room felt suddenly thin and unreal, as though he were watching himself from outside his body, and the fluorescent lights seemed to pulse with menace. He stood up, his hands shaking, and walked directly to the break room, where he found another guard, Ramirez, making coffee. Without preamble, Marco accused him of something petty—of taking his lunch from the fridge weeks ago—and within minutes they were shouting at each other, their voices echoing off the metal lockers. It was a fight Marco didn't actually believe in, but it burned away the dissociation, replaced it with hot anger that felt like being alive.

Catalina noticed the pattern. He would come home agitated, looking for reasons to argue with her about the dishes, about money, about nothing. She began to fear his moods, and he began to fear what would happen if she left him. He had already failed to protect Diego. He could not fail at his marriage too. Yet the more he tried to control it, the more fragile it seemed. When his mother called to talk about setting up a memorial service, Marco felt that same sickening distance creeping in—the world becoming cotton, his body a puppet. He told his mother he couldn't talk about it, that they should just cremate Diego and move on, and then he picked a fight with Catalina that night, accusing her of being cold and unsupportive, knowing even as he spoke that it wasn't true. The argument burned the dissociation away, but it left Catalina crying in the bedroom, and Marco sat alone in the dark, convinced that he was incapable of being the husband she deserved, that he had somehow already ruined everything by not being the brother Diego needed.

The avoidance had become total. He took different routes home to avoid the street where Diego used to live. He changed the radio station if a song came on that his brother had loved. He stopped answering his mother's calls because hearing her voice triggered the same sense of unreality, and he knew he would come home looking for a fight that would only push Catalina further away. But the more he avoided these reminders, the more his mind seemed to trap him with them. Driving past the highway exit where the accident occurred—even when he tried to take a different route, he sometimes ended up there anyway, his hands white-knuckled on the wheel—he would feel the dissociation creeping in, that terrible floating feeling, and he would have to pull into a gas station and start an argument with the clerk over something meaningless, just to feel solid again. He had come to believe that he was fundamentally broken, that happiness was something that happened to other men, not to him. The future looked like an endless corridor of the same days, the same failures, the same desperate scramble to outrun a grief that was always catching up. What frightened him most was that Catalina would finally see what he already knew—that he was a man who couldn't protect anyone, not even himself.

When he called the therapist's office last week, it was because Catalina had threatened to leave. Marco told the intake coordinator that he needed help, but what he really meant was that he was terrified of losing the last person he had left, and he had no idea how to stop the machinery inside himself that was grinding them both to dust.
